title: Spain and Portugal
lead: Spain's classic regions, its aging words (Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva) and Cava. Then Portugal's Vinho Verde and Douro.

intro.title: THE SPANISH LABEL
intro.text: Spain ranks regions by appellation, then ranks wines by how long they aged.

tiers.name: DOCa
tiers.note: Top tier. Only Rioja and Priorat (DOQ in Catalan).

tiers.name: DO
tiers.note: Rías Baixas, Ribera del Duero, Toro, Rueda, Cava.

tiers.name: Aging terms
tiers.note: Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva: longer aging, in order.

court.outcome: After studying this section, a student will know the location, general climate, grape variety, and style of the Rías Baixas DO. After studying this section, a student will know the general location, climate, grape varieties, styles, and label language of Rioja. After studying this section, a student will know the major DOs within Castilla y León, the grape varieties used, and styles of wine produced. After studying this section, a student will understand the general location, styles, and grape varieties of the Cava DO and Priorat DOCa. After studying this section, a student will know the location of Portugal on a map and Portugal's important wine regions and grape varieties.

sections.name: Spain: law and aging words

lines.label: Appellations
lines.text: DOCa is the top tier. Only Rioja and Priorat hold it. Most other quality regions are DO.

lines.label: Aging
lines.text: Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva rise in order of minimum time in oak and bottle. The Court says exact times aren't needed at this level.

know: Rioja was Spain's first DOCa, in 1991.
Crianza < Reserva < Gran Reserva, by minimum aging time.
Gran Reserva is typically made only in the best vintages.
Rioja's youngest category is Generic: 1-2 year wines. The Court calls young styles Joven.
Sherry belongs to the fortified-wine chapter.

visuals.note: Rioja's rules for red wine. The Court lists the same minimums for Ribera del Duero.

sections.name: Rioja

lines.label: Place
lines.text: North central Spain, on the Ebro River. The Cantabrian Mountains block rain, so the climate is continental.

lines.label: Style
lines.text: Dry reds from Tempranillo and whites from Viura, traditionally aged in American oak. Styles run from young and fresh to ageable.

know: Rioja is a DOCa.
Red Rioja is based on Tempranillo. White Rioja is based on Viura.
Traditional Rioja is aged in American oak.
The three zones are Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa and Rioja Oriental.
Some modern producers use French oak and skip the Crianza and Reserva labels.
Rioja sits in the foothills of the Cantabrian and Pyrenees mountains.

sections.name: Ribera del Duero, Toro, Rueda

lines.label: Place
lines.text: Castilla y León, on a high plateau (the meseta) along the Duero River. Hot days, cold nights, harsh winters.

lines.label: Style
lines.text: Tempranillo reds in Ribera del Duero and Toro. Fresh whites in Rueda.

know: In Ribera del Duero, Tempranillo is also called Tinto Fino or Tinta del País.
Ribera del Duero reds must be at least 75% Tempranillo.
Ribera vineyards sit at about 720 to over 1,000 meters.
Toro makes ripe, concentrated Tempranillo reds.
Rueda makes fresh whites from Verdejo and Sauvignon Blanc.
Ribera del Duero uses the same aging words as Rioja: Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva.

sections.name: Rías Baixas

lines.label: Place
lines.text: Galicia, in northwest 'Green Spain' on the Atlantic. Maritime, humid and cooler than the rest of Spain.

lines.label: Style
lines.text: Dry, crisp, aromatic whites from Albariño, made in stainless steel, often aged on the lees.

know: Rías Baixas means 'low estuaries'.
A wine labelled Albariño must be 100% Albariño.
Albariño is about 96% of the grapes grown here.
Albariño is a classic match for simply prepared shellfish.
Vines are trained on a high canopy because of the humidity.

visuals.title: Albariño on the label
visuals.text: A Rías Baixas wine labelled Albariño must be made only from Albariño.

sections.name: Priorat

lines.label: Place
lines.text: Catalonia, near Barcelona. Hot, dry Mediterranean climate on steep, terraced slate slopes.

lines.label: Style
lines.text: Powerful, intense, spicy reds based on Garnacha, often aged in French oak and blended with international grapes.

know: Priorat is one of only two DOCa regions (DOQ in Catalan).
Llicorella soil lets vines dig deep for water.
Priorat is a modern style that made a big impact fast. Its revival began in the late 1980s.
Slopes are too steep for machines, and yields are very low.

sections.name: Cava

lines.label: Method
lines.text: Traditional-method sparkling wine: the second fermentation happens in the bottle.

lines.label: Place
lines.text: Cava can be made in several parts of Spain, but most comes from Penedès in Catalonia.

know: The gyropalette, a Spanish invention, is used instead of riddling by hand.
Cava de Guarda ages at least 9 months on the lees.
Cava Reserva ages at least 18 months; Gran Reserva 30 months.
Sant Sadurní d'Anoia is called the Cava capital.
Catalonia is in northeastern Spain; most Cava grows on high Pyrenees-foothill sites, where altitude keeps it moderate.

visuals.note: Reserva, Gran Reserva and Paraje are grouped as Cava de Guarda Superior.

sections.name: Portugal at a glance

lines.label: Place
lines.text: On the Iberian Peninsula, on Spain's western border, with the Atlantic to the west. Maritime in the north, warm continental inland toward Spain.

lines.label: DOPs
lines.text: The Court names four: Vinho Verde, Douro, Porto and Madeira. Porto and Madeira are fortified.

know: Portugal is on Spain's western border; the Atlantic is its own western border.
The climate runs from maritime in the north to warm continental inland.
The interior is very mountainous, and the Douro River is Spain's Duero.
Four DOPs to know: Vinho Verde, Douro, Porto, Madeira.
Madeira is a fortified white, made dry, medium dry or sweet, from Sercial, Verdelho, Bual and Malmsey.

sections.name: Vinho Verde

lines.label: Place
lines.text: Northwest Portugal, from the Minho River south to the Vouga. Cool, green, rainy and Atlantic.

lines.label: Style
lines.text: Low alcohol with a slight fizz. Mostly white.

know: Alvarinho is the same grape as Spain's Albariño.
Vinho Verde is Portugal's largest denomination.
Monção e Melgaço is shielded from the Atlantic and makes fuller wines.
Soils are mostly granite.

sections.name: Douro, and Port in brief

lines.label: Place
lines.text: Northeast Portugal, steep terraces of schist along the Douro River. Mountains block Atlantic winds: cold winters, hot dry summers.

lines.label: Style
lines.text: Bold, dry red wines, and Port, a sweet fortified red. Port is covered in the fortified chapter.

know: Douro soil is schist.
Touriga Nacional is the key red grape for Douro and Port.
The Douro was demarcated in 1756, the oldest demarcated region in the world.
Port is fortified during fermentation with grape brandy, which leaves it sweet.
Subregions west to east: Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo, Douro Superior.

items.text: Granite, ringed by mountains. Touriga Nacional, Encruzado

items.name: Alentejo
items.text: Hot, dry plains. Antão Vaz, Aragonez, Trincadeira

mixups.why: Same grape. Albariño in Spain's Rías Baixas, Alvarinho in Portugal's Vinho Verde.
Same river. Duero in Spain (Ribera del Duero, Toro, Rueda), Douro in Portugal (Douro, Port).
Both age a year in oak in Rioja. Reserva needs 3 years in total; Crianza needs 2.
Not different grapes: local names for Tempranillo in Ribera del Duero.

facts.fact: Court Course Guide Section 7: Spain (Rías Baixas, Rioja, Ribera del Duero, Toro, Rueda, Cava, Priorat) and Portugal (Vinho Verde, Douro).
Court Course Guide Section 10 covers fortified wines: Sherry, Port, Madeira, Vins Doux Naturels.
Sherry is in the Court's Fortified Wines subject: southwest Spain, Jerez-Xérès-Sherry; albariza (chalk) soil; Palomino, Moscatel, Pedro Ximénez; fortified after fermentation.
Rías Baixas (Intro): northwest Iberian Peninsula, 'Green Spain'; maritime, humid, cooler than the rest of Spain; Atlantic Ocean and Miño/Minho River; Rías Baixas means 'low estuaries'.
Rías Baixas winemaking (Intro): modern technology, stainless steel; lees aging common. Grape: Albariño. Wines labelled Albariño must be 100% Albariño. Style: dry, crisp, aromatic whites.

Rías Baixas: high canopy trellising because of humidity is in the Introductory column; granite soil and the shellfish pairing (Albariño with simply prepared shellfish and bivalves) are in the Certified column.
D.O. Rías Baixas: Galicia, mostly Pontevedra; regulating council set up 1988; five sub-zones Val do Salnés, O Rosal, Ribeira do Ulla, Condado do Tea, Soutomaior; 4,184 ha in over 22,500 plots.
Rías Baixas: Albariño is 96% of grape production and 95% of wine production; traditional pergola training.

Rioja (Intro): north central Spain; Cantabrian Mountains create a rain shadow; continental; foothills of Cantabrian and Pyrenees; Ebro River. Traditionally aged in American oak. Grapes: Viura (white), Tempranillo and Garnacha (red); Mazuelo, Graciano, Malvasia, Garnacha Blanca in the Certified column.

La Rioja DOCa (Intro): dry red (tinto) wines from Tempranillo and white (blanco) wines from Viura. Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva are aging tiers, in ascending order, by minimum time in oak and bottle; actual times are not necessary at Intro level.

Certified column: Rioja subzones Rioja Alta, Rioja Oriental, Rioja Alavesa; Joven; Viñedo Singular; carbonic maceration common on Joven. Rioja tinto: Crianza min 2 years incl. 1 in oak; Reserva min 3 years incl. 1 in oak; Gran Reserva min 5 years incl. 2 in oak.

Certified column: Gran Reserva is typically only made in the best vintages; some modern producers use French oak and skip Crianza/Reserva/Gran Reserva labels; Bordeaux and Rioja relationship during phylloxera.
Rioja has been a DO since 1925 and a Qualified Designation of Origin (DOCa) since 1991, the first in Spain; only two meet the standard nationally.

Rioja aging: Generic = 1-2 year wines keeping fresh fruit. Crianza = minimum 2 years, at least 1 year in 225-litre oak barrels (whites and rosés 6 months in barrel). Reserva = minimum 3 years, at least 1 in barrel plus at least 6 months in bottle. Gran Reserva = minimum 5 years, 2 in barrel plus 2 in bottle.
Rioja origin labels: Viñedo Singular (since 2017), Vino de Zona (Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa, Rioja Oriental), Vino de Municipio (144 municipalities).
Rioja is divided into Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa and Rioja Oriental, on both sides of the Ebro; about 100 km west to east; Atlantic and Mediterranean climates; more than 66,000 ha.
Rioja grows 14 grape varieties; Tempranillo occupies most plantings; Viura has been the main white since the 1970s.
Rioja red: lighter, fruitier young reds may be fermented whole-bunch (carbonic maceration); aging mentions require 225-litre oak barrels.

Castilla y León (Intro): north central Spain; Cantabrian rain shadow; continental with extreme seasonal and day-night shifts; high-altitude meseta; Duero River (Douro in Portugal). Grapes: Verdejo, Sauvignon Blanc, Tempranillo. Toro DO: mainly Tempranillo reds, ripe and concentrated. Ribera del Duero DO: Tempranillo-based, young to long-aged in American or French oak. Rueda DO: fresh whites from Verdejo and Sauvignon Blanc.

Certified column: Tempranillo synonyms Tinta del País and Tinta de Toro; Bierzo DO (Mencía); Ribera tinto Crianza 2 yrs (1 oak), Reserva 3 yrs (1 oak), Gran Reserva 5 yrs (2 oak). Producers: Vega Sicilia, Pesquera, Pingus.
Ribera del Duero: vineyards from 720 to over 1,000 m on the northern meseta; 115 km along the Duero; 25,035 ha; over 300 wineries.
Ribera del Duero climate: Mediterranean with strong continentality: dry summers, long harsh winters, under 400 mm rain a year, range -20°C to 42°C.
Ribera del Duero: Tempranillo, also called Tinta del País or Tinto Fino, is the main grape; main white is Albillo Mayor.
Ribera del Duero reds: at least 95% red grapes and at least 75% Tempranillo (Tinto Fino/Tinta del País); categories young, Roble, Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva.

Catalonia (Intro): northeastern Spain, Pyrenees foothills, near Barcelona. Priorat: hot, dry Mediterranean; steep terraced slopes; llicorella soil lets vines dig deep for water; modern winemaking with French oak. Cava: moderate due to altitude; traditional method; the gyropalette (a Spanish invention) replaces hand riddling. Cava grapes Xarel-lo, Parellada, Macabeo. Priorat grapes Garnacha, Cariñena, international varieties.

Cava DO (Intro): traditional-method sparkling, white and rosado, from native grapes. Priorat DOCa: mainly still dry reds from Garnacha, Cariñena and international grapes. Certified: Cava covers all of Spain but most is made in Penedès; Cava de Guarda min 9 months on lees; Reserva min 18 months. Priorat: no mechanization, bush-vine (Gobelet) training, low yields.

Priorat (Intro): powerful, intense, spicy Garnacha-based blend, often French oak, with international grapes; a modern, not traditional, style that made a big impact quickly. Certified: Gratallops project; producers Clos Mogador, Álvaro Palacios, Clos Erasmus.

DOQ Priorat: small mountainous region in Tarragona; Montsant massif to the north; Siurana river; 17,629 ha area with 2,196.8 ha of vines; villages include Gratallops and la Morera de Montsant (Scala Dei).

Priorat: vines from 100 to 750 m; steep slopes (costers) and narrow terraces that machines can't work; yields under 1 kg per vine; Cariñena (Carinyena) and Garnacha (Garnatxa) are the key native grapes.
Priorat is 'the territory of slate'.
Carthusian monks of Scala Dei brought winemaking to Priorat in the 12th century; a new cycle of prosperity began at the end of the 1980s.

Cava aging: Cava de Guarda minimum 9 months; Cava de Guarda Superior: Reserva over 18 months, Gran Reserva 30 months, Cava de Paraje Calificado over 36 months. Gran Reserva and Paraje come only in Brut Nature, Extra Brut and Brut.
Cava de Guarda name approved in July 2020; second fermentation in the bottle (traditional method).
Cava de Guarda Superior grapes must come from specific vineyards and be organically grown; Reserva minimum raised to 18 months in 2020.
Cava's origins are in Penedès, especially Sant Sadurní d'Anoia, the 'Cava capital'; Cava can also be made in some other regions; four main areas; sub-zones approved 2020.
Wine Folly (secondary): Spain's DOP tiers include Vino de Pago, DOCa and DO; Rioja and Priorat are the only DOCa; IGP/Vino de la Tierra is the next tier down.

Portugal (Intro): western border of Spain; maritime north on the Atlantic, warm continental interior; Douro River (Duero in Spain); very mountainous interior. Douro and Porto DOP soil: schist. Vinho Verde: low alcohol, slight effervescence. Porto and Madeira: fortified. Grapes: Alvarinho (Vinho Verde), Touriga Nacional (Douro and Porto). DOPs: Vinho Verde, Douro, Porto, Madeira. Styles: Douro bold dry reds; Porto fortified sweet red.
Portugal Certified column: Douro subregions Cima Corgo, Baixo Corgo, Douro Superior; Dão, Alentejo, Bairrada DOPs; terraces on mountainsides; Single Quinta; lagares (stone fermenters).
Port (Intro, fortified chapter): same area as Douro DOP; fortified during fermentation; Touriga Nacional; Ruby (Ruby, LBV, Single Quinta, Vintage) and Aged Tawny (10, 20, 30, 40 year).

Douro: Northeast Portugal, about 250,000 ha region, three sub-regions (Lower Corgo, Upper Corgo, Upper Douro); mostly schist; Marão and Montemuro mountains block Atlantic winds; very cold winters, hot dry summers.
Douro reds come from native grapes such as Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Aragonez), Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão, mostly blends.
Port is fortified by stopping fermentation with grape brandy (benefício); usually 19-22% alcohol.
The Douro Demarcated Region is the oldest demarcated and regulated region in the world (1756) and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Douro: thousands of terraces on steep slopes; UNESCO World Heritage; Baixo Corgo coolest and rainiest; Cima Corgo the heart; Douro Superior largest, hottest, driest. 1756: Companhia Geral da Agricultura das Vinhas do Alto Douro created; Port aged in Vila Nova de Gaia.
Vinho Verde: Demarcated Region since 1908; nine subregions including Monção e Melgaço; DO covers still and sparkling white, red and rosé.

Vinho Verde: largest Portuguese denomination, about 24,000 ha, northwest Portugal, bounded north by the Minho; mostly granite soils; Monção e Melgaço is the only subregion protected from direct Atlantic influence, giving fuller wines; white grapes Alvarinho, Arinto, Avesso, Azal, Loureiro, Trajadura.
Dão: surrounded by mountains, poor granite soils, vineyards from 200 to 1,000 m; Encruzado white; Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro, Jaen, Tinta Roriz red.
Wine Folly (secondary): the vast majority of Vinho Verde wines are white; six grapes form the backbone of the whites: Alvarinho, Arinto, Azal, Avesso, Loureiro, Trajadura.

Alentejo: rolling plains covering almost a third of mainland Portugal; hot, dry Mediterranean climate with continental influence; eight sub-regions; whites Antão Vaz, Arinto, Roupeiro; reds Alicante Bouschet, Aragonez, Castelão, Trincadeira.
Wine Folly (secondary): Albariño's two main homes are Rías Baixas in Spain and Vinho Verde in Portugal, where it is called Alvarinho.
Rías Baixas (Introductory column, checked on the rendered page): high canopy trellising because of humidity; bodies of water are the Atlantic Ocean and the Miño River (Minho in Portuguese).
Rioja (Introductory column): physical features are the foothills of the Cantabrian and Pyrenees Mountains and the Ebro River.

Castilla y León (Introductory column): north central Spain; the Cantabrian Mountains create a rain shadow. Label terms for Ribera del Duero: Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva, in ascending order of minimum time in oak and bottle.

Catalonia (Introductory column): northeastern Spain, in the foothills of the Pyrenees, near the Mediterranean Sea and the city of Barcelona. Cava: moderate climate due to altitude where most Cava is made; high-altitude sites in the Pyrenees.
Priorat (Introductory column, History & Lore): a modern Spanish wine, not a traditional style; it made a big impact in a short time and is highly respected.

Portugal (Introductory column): Madeira DOP is fortified; Madeira white grapes Sercial, Verdelho, Bual, Malmsey; style fortified dry, medium dry and sweet white wines. Porto DOP: fortified, sweet red wine. Tinta Negra (Madeira) is in the Certified column.

Wines of Portugal: Madeira sits in the North Atlantic; its four noble grapes Sercial, Verdelho, Boal and Malvasia are all white and made dry, medium dry, semi-sweet and sweet respectively; Tinta Negra is over 80% of the harvest; vines grow on small terraces on steep slopes; soils are volcanic.

unverified: Spain's national aging minimums (outside Rioja and Ribera del Duero) were not confirmed from Spanish law or the Ministry; only Rioja's regulator and the Court were used.

Wine Folly's Spain page gives Rioja Reserva as '1 year in oak/2 in bottle' and Gran Reserva as '2 years in oak/3 in bottle', which conflicts with the Rioja regulator (Reserva 3 years total incl. 1 in oak and 6 months in bottle; Gran Reserva 5 years incl. 2 in oak and 2 in bottle). The regulator's figures are used.
Rioja's regulator now names its youngest category 'Generic'; the word Joven comes from the Court (Certified column). No official definition of Joven was fetched.
Toro DO and Rueda DO regulator sites were not fetched; their facts come from the Court only.

Ribera del Duero's 'Nuestros vinos' page shows '36 months, 12 in barrel' under an unlabelled image near the rosé section; it was not used. The Court's Ribera minimums (Certified column) match Rioja's.
The Rías Baixas statistics page is age-gated and could not be read; Albariño share (96% of grapes) comes from the D.O. 'Our wines' page.
Counts of Spanish DOs and Vinos de Pago were not confirmed from an official source and are left out.
Sherry styles (Fino, Manzanilla, Amontillado, Oloroso, PX) were not researched here: the Court puts Sherry in the Fortified Wines subject (course Section 10), so this chapter only points to it.
Dão and Alentejo appear in the Court's Certified column for Portugal; they are included as context only. Port details beyond the basics are left to the fortified chapter.
Rioja soils (calcareous clay, ferrous clay, alluvial) sit in the Court's Certified column (checked on the rendered PDF page, Nov 2 2026), so they stay out of this Level 1 chapter.
Court column split (Introductory vs Certified) was read from the PDF's text positions and re-checked against rendered page images on Nov 2 2026 (pages 37-46).
Madeira grape names: the Court writes Bual and Malmsey; Wines of Portugal writes Boal and Malvasia. Both spellings are given.
The Court lists Madeira DOP under Portugal at the Introductory level; this chapter covers it briefly and leaves the detail to the fortified chapter.
The 'Portugal at a glance' video is from Wines of Portugal (the official generic body); it is a brand film, not a lesson, so it is a light intro only.

video.title: 5 Spanish Red Wines You Must Try

read.bigIdea: Spain ranks the place, then how long the wine aged.
read.where: The top tier is **DOCa**, and only **Rioja** and **Priorat** hold it. Priorat’s label says **DOQ**. Most other quality regions, like Rías Baixas, Ribera del Duero and Cava, are **DO**. For the aging words, the Court only asks you to know their order, not the exact times.

stops.name: Generic (Joven)
stops.text: Rioja calls its youngest wines **Generic**: 1-2 years old, keeping their fresh fruit. The Court calls young styles **Joven**.

stops.name: Crianza
stops.text: A red Rioja **Crianza** ages at least **2 years**, with 1 in oak.

stops.name: Reserva
stops.text: A red Rioja **Reserva** ages at least **3 years**, with 1 in oak and at least 6 months in bottle.

stops.name: Gran Reserva
stops.text: At least **5 years** in Rioja, with 2 in oak and 2 in bottle. It’s typically made only in the **best vintages**.

read.visualIntro: Rioja’s red-wine minimums, side by side:
read.mixup: **Crianza** and **Reserva** both spend a year in oak in Rioja. Reserva needs 3 years in total; Crianza needs 2.
read.sayIt: This Rioja Reserva aged at least three years before release.

keyPoints.line: is the main red grape of Rioja.
is the main white grape of Rioja.

read.bigIdea: Rioja is Tempranillo, aged in American oak.
read.where: Rioja sits in **north central Spain**, along the **Ebro River**. The **Cantabrian Mountains** block the rain, so the climate is **continental**. It was Spain’s first **DOCa**, and its three zones are **Rioja Alta**, **Rioja Alavesa** and **Rioja Oriental**. Its vineyards sit in the foothills of the **Cantabrian** and **Pyrenees** mountains.

stops.name: Red Rioja
stops.text: Based on **Tempranillo**, which fills most of the vineyards, with **Garnacha** as a partner. Styles run from young and fresh to long-aged.

stops.name: White Rioja
stops.text: Based on **Viura**, Rioja’s main white grape since the 1970s.

stops.name: Traditional or modern
stops.text: Traditional Rioja ages in **American oak**. Some modern producers use **French oak** and skip the Crianza and Reserva labels.

read.mixup: Traditional **Rioja** ages in American oak. Modern **Priorat** leans on French oak.
read.sayIt: A Rioja is Spanish Tempranillo, traditionally aged in American oak.

keyPoints.line: is Ribera del Duero’s local name for Tempranillo.
is the least Tempranillo a Ribera del Duero red can have.

read.bigIdea: Three wines from Spain’s high plateau on the Duero.
read.where: These three DOs are in **Castilla y León**, on a high plateau called the **meseta**, along the **Duero River**. Seasons and day-night temperatures swing hard, and winters are long and harsh. Ribera’s vineyards sit at about **720 to over 1,000 meters**. The region is in **north central Spain**, in the **rain shadow** of the **Cantabrian Mountains**.

stops.name: Ribera del Duero
stops.text: Here Tempranillo is called **Tinto Fino** or **Tinta del País**. Reds must be at least **75%** Tempranillo, from young to long-aged in American or French oak. Labels use the same aging words as Rioja: **Crianza**, **Reserva**, **Gran Reserva**.

stops.name: Toro
stops.text: Mainly **Tempranillo** reds, **ripe and concentrated**.

stops.name: Rueda
stops.text: Fresh whites from **Verdejo** and **Sauvignon Blanc**.

read.mixup: **Tinto Fino** and **Tinta del País** aren’t new grapes. They’re local names for **Tempranillo**.
read.sayIt: Ribera del Duero is Tempranillo from Spain’s high plateau.

read.bigIdea: Rías Baixas is Spain’s Atlantic white-wine corner.
read.where: Rías Baixas is in **Galicia**, in northwest **“Green Spain”** on the **Atlantic**. The climate is **maritime**, humid and cooler than the rest of Spain. The name means **“low estuaries.”** Its river is the **Miño** (Minho in Portugal), and vines are trained on a **high canopy** because of the **humidity**.

stops.name: The grape
stops.text: **Albariño** is about 96% of the grapes grown here. A wine labeled Albariño must be **100% Albariño**.

stops.name: The cellar
stops.text: Modern winemaking in **stainless steel**, often with **lees aging**.

stops.name: The glass
stops.text: **Dry, crisp, aromatic** whites. A classic match for simply prepared **shellfish**.

read.visualIntro: One rule to remember on the label:
read.mixup: **Albariño** in Spain and **Alvarinho** in Portugal’s Vinho Verde are the same grape.
read.sayIt: Rías Baixas Albariño: crisp and aromatic, great with shellfish.

read.bigIdea: Priorat is Spain’s modern, powerful red.
read.where: Priorat is in **Catalonia**, near **Barcelona**. The climate is **hot and dry Mediterranean**, and vines grow on **steep, terraced slopes**. The soil is **llicorella**, which lets vines dig deep for water.

stops.name: The grapes
stops.text: **Garnacha** and **Cariñena** are the key native grapes, often blended with **international grapes**.

stops.name: The land
stops.text: Slopes and narrow terraces are too steep for machines. Yields are **very low**: under 1 kg per vine.

stops.name: The style
stops.text: **Powerful, intense and spicy**, often aged in **French oak**. It’s a **modern** style that made a big impact fast; the revival began in the late 1980s. Today it is **highly respected**.

read.visualIntro: Spain’s two DOCa regions, side by side:
read.sayIt: Priorat is a big, spicy Garnacha blend from steep hills near Barcelona.

read.bigIdea: Cava is Spain’s traditional-method sparkling wine.
read.where: Cava can be made in several parts of Spain, but most comes from **Penedès** in **Catalonia**. The town of **Sant Sadurní d’Anoia** is called the **Cava capital**. Catalonia is in **northeastern Spain**, in the **Pyrenees foothills** near the Mediterranean and **Barcelona**. Most Cava grows on **high-altitude** sites, where the climate stays **moderate**.

stops.name: The grapes
stops.text: White and rosado Cava come from native grapes: **Xarel-lo**, **Parellada** and **Macabeo**.

stops.name: In the bottle
stops.text: The **second fermentation** happens in the bottle. That’s the **traditional method**.

stops.name: Riddling
stops.text: A Spanish invention, the **gyropalette**, replaces riddling by hand.

stops.name: Aging
stops.text: **Cava de Guarda** ages at least **9 months**. **Reserva** needs 18 months and **Gran Reserva** 30.

read.visualIntro: The longer on the lees, the higher the tier:
read.mixup: **Reserva** on a Cava means at least 18 months on the lees. On a red Rioja, it means at least 3 years of aging.
read.sayIt: Cava is Spanish sparkling wine, with its bubbles made in the bottle.

video.title: Wines of Portugal - a world of difference

keyPoints.line: of Spain: Portugal is Iberia’s Atlantic side.
fill the interior, which runs warm and continental.
to know: Vinho Verde, Douro, Porto and Madeira.
is a fortified white, made from dry to sweet.

read.where: Portugal sits on the **Iberian Peninsula**, on **Spain’s western border**, with the **Atlantic** as its own western edge. The north is **maritime**; inland, toward Spain, it turns **warm continental**. The interior is **very mountainous**, and the **Douro River** is the same river as Spain’s **Duero**.

stops.name: Vinho Verde
stops.text: **Low alcohol** with a **slight fizz**, from grapes like **Alvarinho**.

stops.name: Douro
stops.text: **Bold, dry reds** from grapes like **Touriga Nacional**, grown on **schist**.

stops.name: Porto
stops.text: A **fortified, sweet red** from the same area as the Douro wines.

stops.name: Madeira
stops.text: A **fortified white**, made **dry**, **medium dry** or **sweet**. The four classic grapes are **Sercial**, **Verdelho**, **Bual** and **Malmsey** (Boal and Malvasia in Portuguese).

read.mixup: **Porto** and **Douro** come from the same area. Porto is fortified and sweet; Douro reds are dry.
read.sayIt: Madeira is a fortified wine from a Portuguese island, made dry to sweet.

keyPoints.line: is the same grape as Spain’s Albariño.
and a slight fizz are the Vinho Verde style.

read.bigIdea: Vinho Verde is Portugal’s light, low-alcohol white.
read.where: Vinho Verde is in **northwest Portugal**, bounded to the north by the **Minho River**. The north is **maritime**, on the Atlantic, and the soils are mostly **granite**. It’s Portugal’s **largest** denomination.

stops.name: The style
stops.text: **Low alcohol** with a **slight fizz**. The vast majority is white.

stops.name: The grapes
stops.text: **Alvarinho** is the key grape. **Loureiro**, **Arinto**, Avesso, Azal and Trajadura are the other main whites.

stops.name: Monção e Melgaço
stops.text: The only subregion shielded from the Atlantic, so its wines are **fuller**.

read.mixup: **Alvarinho** is Portugal’s name for Spain’s **Albariño**. Same grape, two labels.
read.sayIt: Vinho Verde is light and low in alcohol, with a little spritz.

read.bigIdea: The Douro makes bold dry reds, and Port.
read.where: The Douro is in **northeast Portugal**, on steep terraces of **schist** along the **Douro River**. Mountains block the Atlantic winds, so winters are very cold and summers are **hot and dry**. In Spain, the same river is called the **Duero**.

stops.name: Douro reds
stops.text: **Bold, dry reds**, mostly blends of native grapes like **Touriga Nacional**, **Touriga Franca** and **Tinta Roriz**.

stops.name: Port
stops.text: Grape brandy is added **during fermentation**, which stops it and leaves the wine **sweet**. Port gets its own lesson in the fortified chapter.
The Douro was demarcated in **1756**, the **oldest demarcated region** in the world.

read.visualIntro: Heading east, the valley gets hotter and drier:
read.mixup: **Douro** is the river in Portugal. **Duero** is the same river in Spain, home of Ribera del Duero.
read.sayIt: A Douro red: bold and dry, from the same grapes as Port.
